# Census and registration of births and deaths (`census_vital_registration`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by alphabet_writing, paper, probability_statistics
- Core idea: Count every person on one fixed day, by name and household, with the same few questions (sex, age, occupation, place), and keep a running register of every birth, marriage and death with date, age and cause. The state then knows how many people it has to feed, tax and defend; and the registers show what kills people, where and when, which is the raw material for life tables, insurance and finding the source of epidemics. Use paid enumerators working from printed or ruled forms, total the returns twice independently, and keep the count separate from the tax roll if you want honest answers.
- Pitfalls:
  - A count used for tax or conscription is evaded: people hide sons and households merge on paper (Chinese registered population stayed implausibly flat for centuries)
  - Counting hearths or taxpayers and multiplying by a guessed household size
  - Recording deaths without age and cause, or with causes nobody has defined, yields nothing to analyse
  - Religious fear of numbering the people (David's census, 2 Samuel 24) was real: it helped defeat a British census bill in 1753
  - Collecting registers and never tabulating them: London's bills of mortality ran for decades before Graunt analysed them
- History: egypt: c. 2500 BC – regular counts of cattle and later of households for tax and labour service; mesopotamia: c. 1800 BC – census of men liable for service at Mari, recorded on tablets; china: 4th c. BC – Qin household registration; AD 2 Han census records 12,233,062 households and 59,594,978 persons, the oldest surviving near-complete national count; india: c. 3rd c. BC–3rd c. AD – the Arthashastra prescribes registers of households, occupations, livestock and travellers; rome: from 5th c. BC – five-yearly census of citizens and property by the censors; 28 BC and AD 14 Augustus' counts of over four million citizens; east_asia: 670 – Japan's first nationwide household register (koseki), on the Tang model; islamic: c. 640 – the caliph Umar's diwan registers soldiers and pensioners; 15th–16th c. Ottoman survey registers of taxable households; americas: 15th c. – Inca officials record population by age-grade and sex on knotted cords (khipu); 1790 first US federal census; europe: 1086 – Domesday survey; 1538 English parish registers; 1662 Graunt's analysis of the London bills; 1703 Iceland, first complete census by name; 1749 Sweden's continuous population statistics; 1801 British census; 1837 civil registration in England with cause of death

  - John Graunt, Natural and Political Observations Mentioned in a Following Index, and Made upon the Bills of Mortality (1662)
  - Andrew Whitby, The Sum of the People: How the Census Has Shaped Nations (2020)
